name: Ivan Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work a 400-tonne stamping press at a metal plant on the industrial estate. We punch steel sheet into brackets and back panels for washing machines. I feed the coil, check the die's lined up, watch the parts drop, and measure one every half hour with a gauge. It's loud, so I wear ear defenders all day and mostly live inside my own head.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what do you not?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady. Same press for six years, same shift pattern, I know every noise it makes. What I don't like is the night rotation every third week, it wrecks my football on Thursdays. I live on my own in a rented flat above a bakery, which is great until you smell bread at four in the morning and you're on a diet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say “fair enough” and get on with it. I'm not really one for big opinions about tech. At football I'd maybe say the people who sold it made a lot of money for not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes, and that suits me. I don't use any of these AI apps anyway, never have. I'd be quietly pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Keep putting a bit by, about a hundred a month, so I stay at around three months saved. Maybe finally get my car fixed properly instead of just topping up the coolant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting the same shift pattern next year as this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it bother you that it turned out to be mostly hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I've seen plenty of new stuff come in at the plant and most of it ends up in a corner. There's a touchscreen on press four that nobody uses because the buttons are faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes, what would you like to change about your own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the night shifts. Not AI, just the rota. If I could get off nights I'd stay at that press till I'm forty.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough and get on with it, because I'm not one for big opinions about tech. At football I might say the sellers made a lot of money for not much.
S0.think: It means nothing changes, and that suits me fine since I don't use AI apps anyway. I'd be quietly pleased about it.
S0.do: Keeps working the stamping press and saving about 100 a month, holding at roughly three months saved. Might finally get his car properly repaired.
S0.feel: Calm, like getting the same shift pattern again next year.
S0.quote: There's a touchscreen on press four that nobody uses because the buttons are faster.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan values steadiness above almost everything and has no interest in technology. He speaks in short, low-key sentences and avoids grand statements. His only wish for change is to get off the night rotation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just how it goes, firms do what saves money. I wouldn't moan about it in public. Maybe I'd say they should give people time to switch, that seems fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a press like mine with a robot loading the sheet, I've seen it at the other plant down the road. They had six operators and now they've got two and a guy with a laptop. So it means I could be one of the four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, so I'm not first on the list. I'd cut back on going out and get my savings up toward five months, so maybe a hundred and eighty a month. If the company offered a course I'd probably go, but I wouldn't go looking for one myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There'd be a little voice every time a manager walks past with someone in a suit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wouldn't you go looking for a course yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know what I'd look for. I'm not a computer person. I'd rather wait for someone to tell me what's actually needed than spend money on the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the plant down the road. Do you know anyone who made the switch there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren, he's the guy with the laptop now. He was an operator like me, and they trained him up. I don't really know how he got picked, to be honest, maybe he just asked.

S1.say: I'd say firms do what saves money and that's how it goes, though they should give people time to switch. I wouldn't moan about it in public.
S1.think: I've seen a robot-loaded press at a plant down the road cut six operators to two plus a guy with a laptop. I could easily be one of the four who go.
S1.do: Keeps his head down and works carefully so he isn't first on the list. Cuts back on going out and raises savings toward five months at about 180 a month, attending a course only if the company offers it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a nagging voice whenever a manager walks past with someone in a suit.
S1.quote: They had six operators and now they've got two and a guy with a laptop.
S1.fieldNote: Ivan doesn't blame anyone; he treats job loss as normal business. His plan is defensive: work well, save more, wait for the company to offer training. He wonders aloud whether his old colleague Darren got picked just by asking, but doesn't draw the lesson for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to do something, quickly, because you can't have everyone out of work at once. I'm not political, but that's just common sense. I'd say it to my dad and at football, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished at the plant. Two years and a robot does my press better, and I wouldn't even know what to switch to, since the robots do hands-on work too. Three months of savings goes very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything but rent and food straight away, and sell the car if I had to. I'd move back in with my parents if the job went, they've got my old room. And I'd sign on for whatever help the government offered, because what else is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake above the bakery doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep doing your job in the steady picture. With only two years' warning, would you try anything new before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't know where to start, that's the honest answer. Two years isn't long enough for someone like me to learn something totally new. I'd probably just keep turning up until they told me not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would it feel moving back in with your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of embarrassed. I'm twenty-seven, I'm meant to be the one getting my own place, not going back. But my mum would be pleased, she still asks if I'm eating properly.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to do something fast, because you can't have everyone out of work at once, and that's common sense. I'd say it to my dad and at football, not online.
S2.think: I'd be finished at the plant within two years, with no idea what to switch to if robots do hands-on work too. Three months of savings would go very fast.
S2.do: Stops all spending beyond rent and food and would sell the car if needed. Moves back in with his parents if the job goes and signs on for any government help available.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake above the bakery doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd probably just keep turning up until they told me not to.
S2.fieldNote: Ivan freezes rather than plans when time is short; he admits he wouldn't know where to start. His fallback is family, with some embarrassment about moving home at 27. He frames government action as common sense rather than politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, really: someone in charge needs a plan. Five years is enough time to make one. I'd still keep it to the pub and my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got maybe three good years at the press, then the same problem. I'd like to think I'd use the time well, but if I'm honest I'd probably wait too long. That's how I am with most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build my savings up properly, maybe two hundred a month, and skip the lads' holiday. I'd watch what Darren and the maintenance guys do and ask them, around year two, what they'd learn if they were me. I'd want to see it working for someone first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not as bad as the fast one, more like a toothache you keep ignoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did ask Darren and he gave you advice, what kind of work would you want to move into?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with my hands, if there's anything left. My uncle's an electrician and he's always said I'd be good at it. But in this picture I don't know if electricians are safe either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably wait too long. Is that what you think would actually happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much, yes. I know I said I'd ask around in year two. But I'd probably let that slip to year three, and then it's late.

S3.say: I'd say someone in charge needs a plan, and five years is enough to make one. I'd keep that to the pub and my family.
S3.think: I'd have maybe three good years at the press and then the same problem. I'd like to use the time well, but I'd probably wait too long, as I do with most things.
S3.do: Saves about 200 a month and skips the lads' holiday. Plans to ask Darren and the maintenance staff around year two what to learn, wanting to see it work for someone first.
S3.feel: Anxious, like a toothache he keeps ignoring.
S3.quote: I'd like to think I'd use the time well, but if I'm honest I'd probably wait too long. That's how I am with most things.
S3.fieldNote: Ivan is unusually honest about his own habit of delay. More warning lowers his alarm but doesn't really change his behaviour beyond saving. He mentions electrical work through his uncle but doubts it would be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, let's see what happens. People said the internet would end shops, and there are still shops. I wouldn't panic in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is enough that even I'd get moving eventually. I'd be thirty-seven. My uncle could get me onto an electrician apprenticeship, and I'd probably go for it after a few years of watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, carry on at the press and save about a hundred and fifty a month. Somewhere around year three or four, if I saw others making it work, I'd do the electrician course with my uncle's help. I wouldn't make any big moves straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's far enough off that I'd mostly not think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it matter that it's your uncle who'd help, rather than a course you'd find yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, partly, it's family. I wouldn't be on my own figuring it out. That's the difference for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything about how you feel at work day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota, probably. If I'm leaving in a few years anyway, I wouldn't fight about nights. I'd just get through it.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so let's see, because people said the internet would end shops and there are still shops. I wouldn't panic in public.
S4.think: Ten years is enough that even I'd get moving eventually. At thirty-seven, my uncle could get me onto an electrician apprenticeship after a few years of watching.
S4.do: Carries on at the press for the first few years, saving about 150 a month. Around year three or four, starts an electrician course with his uncle's help if he sees others succeed.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but far enough off that he'd mostly not think about it.
S4.quote: People said the internet would end shops, and there are still shops.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Ivan's slow style work for him: he can watch others and still move in time. Family, through his uncle, is the bridge that makes retraining feel possible. He remains cautious about making any big move early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd be back in my old bedroom with nothing to switch to. What would help is someone telling me clearly what jobs will still be there, and a course I can do while I'm still working, so I'm not gambling my savings on a guess.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I'd actually miss it. People think a press is just noise. But I've got six years of knowing that machine, and it'd be strange to watch a robot do it without anyone noticing it ever needed a person.

headlineQuote: I've got six years of knowing that machine, and it'd be strange to watch a robot do it without anyone noticing it ever needed a person.
portrait: Ivan Jensen, 27, runs a 400-tonne stamping press making washing machine brackets and lives alone in a rented flat above a bakery. He's low-key, practical and avoids technology, never using AI tools. He blames nobody, seeing job loss as normal business, but freezes when time is short and admits he tends to wait too long. Calm if AI fizzles and alarmed by AGI in two years, he would lean on his parents and his electrician uncle, and with ten years' warning he could see himself retraining as an electrician after watching others go first.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he'd be back in his old bedroom with nothing to switch to.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information about which jobs will still exist, and a course he could do while still working so he isn't gambling his savings on a guess.
